en.html:
The situation had developed at considerable speed.
Not from the start, admittedly.

Muramasa appeared at the detention center and reported that she had caught Silver Star's presence. I contacted Kamakura's chief of police, had the release arranged, and emerged from my cell having successfully changed from prisoner Kageaki Minato to police auxiliary Kageaki Minato.

Then, with Muramasa leading, to a poor village near Kamakura.
Up to this point, familiar procedure. No unusual occurrence worth recording.

The thirty minutes after our arrival, however, contained several days' worth of a normal case. Evidently the clocks in this village were fitted with faster hands.

She appeared to understand. Muramasa fell silent.

In flight, speed increased enormously; the warrior could perform to full capacity. Fine maneuvering, on the other hand, was less convenient than with both feet on the ground.

If he followed me up immediately, well and good.
If he ignored me, stayed below, and turned back to his original targets?

Could I stop him successfully a second time?
...Probably a poor wager.

The first move, then, would have to be his. Having settled that, I waited.

Waited.
But—

He did not fly.

The dragoon stayed on the earth, his Gattari cold, no flame issuing from it. His dangerous footwork sought an opening to attack, but every step remained committed to the soil. Not the sky.

Had my refusal to fly made him read too much into things? Did he suspect a trap...?

Possibly. Or perhaps—

The Rokuhara warrior flew away.

Off me—
in an instant—
a considerable distance—

With a single kick of Muramasa's right foot, delivered from underneath him.

At least, so it should have appeared to an observer. An absurd sight. Account for a warrior's weight, account for the man astride us; calculate as carelessly as you please, and that result still would not follow.

The enemy frame had been magnetized. My kick carried the same polarity, and therefore repelled it. With that preparation by Muramasa's Divine Art, the absurdity became possible.

Had the recipient understood the principle?
No time to inquire.

The kick had not inflicted much damage. I knew that. To settle the fight, I must use this opening completely.
I ran.

Muramasa's magnetic plating did not last. A momentary art: maintaining it beyond one second consumed enormous caloric energy. Cancel it, however, and to apply it again I must begin with regulating my breathing.

A fresh start would not remove our disadvantage. My neck wound was serious; as time passed, I would lose blood and heat.
This instant was my only chance.

The Type 88 Dragoon flew again, high, like a puppy hit by a car.

Even so, the enemy had not let go of his sabre. He must have set his stance and steeled his nerve at the moment of impact.

No damage done. And meanwhile our magnetic plating dissolved. The caloric limit.

All that remained was to wait for the outcome.

I secured the height advantage over an enemy who was following the same process, certainly later than me.

Invert. Descend.

A sitting duck, truly. I attacked him one-sidedly.

I had no sword. My fist was the only weapon. What could be destroyed with it was exactly one fatal point.

I closed from his back and punched the waist.

The warrior's posture broke badly, and it did not recover.

The armor spreading around the waist, the horo, is the wing that flight cannot do without. Without it, however much the Gattari burns, it is only noise pollution. The dragoon had lost more than half his wing.

But perhaps the remaining horo tried to do its duty. Falling, the warrior half glided, in a shape between crash and landing, toward the sea of trees below.

...He would probably not die from that. Pursuit was needed.
